actions.body: Recent analysis clarifies that ethical risk in AI stems from the displacement of human responsibility. By situating AI within a history of artificial agency—from automata to computational systems—we observe that responsibility remains anchored in human institutions. Even as agents exhibit 'bounded autonomy' and delegated authority, the epistemic processes of evaluation and ethical judgment are fundamentally human. Interpreting AI outputs as 'signs' within a community of inquiry allows us to locate responsibility not in the machine's internal processing, but in the institutional practices that govern the interpretation and accountability of its outputs. Summary: Moral responsibility for AI outcomes belongs to human actors and institutions, as systems merely operate within delegation frameworks defined by human designers.
actions.lede: Responsibility gaps in AI systems are better understood as failures of human governance and delegation, rather than intrinsic limitations of autonomous machines.
actions.reason: Synthesizing research on human governance and semiotic inquiry to complete the analysis of moral responsibility foundations.
actions.title: Delegated Authority and the Locus of Moral Responsibility
